flashcard_questions.q: How does a linear search begin looking for a target?
flashcard_questions.a: It compares the first item in the list with the target.

flashcard_questions.q: Which searching method works on unsorted data?
What must be true of the data before a binary search works?
flashcard_questions.a: The list must already be sorted.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the smallest number of comparisons a linear search can need?
How many comparisons does a linear search need in the worst case?
flashcard_questions.a: As many comparisons as there are items in the list.

flashcard_questions.q: Which item does a binary search compare with the target first?
flashcard_questions.a: The middle item of the list.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a binary search do when the target is smaller than the middle item?
flashcard_questions.a: It discards the middle item and the whole upper half.

flashcard_questions.q: By how much does each binary search comparison reduce the list?
flashcard_questions.a: It halves the number of items still to check.

flashcard_questions.q: What number of comparisons did the binary search for 45 need?
Roughly how many comparisons does a binary search need on a thousand items?
How many comparisons could a linear search need on a thousand items?
What does doubling the list size add to a binary search?
Why is a binary search not always the better choice?
flashcard_questions.a: It only works on a sorted list, and sorting takes time.

flashcard_questions.q: When is a linear search usually the sensible choice?
flashcard_questions.a: When the data set is small or changes often and is rarely kept in order.

flashcard_questions.q: When does a binary search pay off most?
flashcard_questions.a: When the same sorted list is searched again and again.

notes: 15 cards: 5 algorithm-to-property (prerequisite, first comparison, halving), 5 step-count cards using the lesson's own worked figures, 3 scenario-to-choice, 2 mechanism. Every comparison count is the one the content states, not a general big-O claim.
